s: A media company serves about 300 TB per month of images and video clips to users, mostly in North America and Europe, from Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer in a single Region. Data transfer out to the internet is now the largest line item on the bill. Most of the content is static and is requested many times. Which solution will reduce costs the MOST?
o: Move the static content to Amazon S3 and serve it through an Amazon CloudFront distribution that uses the S3 bucket as its origin with origin access control (OAC).
Put AWS Global Accelerator in front of the Application Load Balancer to route users over the AWS global network.
Buy a Compute Savings Plan for the EC2 instances and move to larger instance types with higher network bandwidth.
Deploy copies of the application in three more Regions and use Amazon Route 53 latency-based routing.

w.y: Data transfer from AWS origins (S3, EC2, ALB) to CloudFront is free, so the company pays only CloudFront delivery, which at this volume costs less per GB than EC2 internet data transfer for North American and European viewers (CloudFront flat-rate plans can lower it further). Edge caching offloads repeated requests from the origin, and moving static files to S3 takes load off the EC2 fleet.

o.A: Correct. Origin fetches are free, caching offloads the origin, and CloudFront delivery is cheaper per GB than EC2 internet data transfer in these geographies at this volume.
o.B: Global Accelerator improves performance but adds a fixed fee and a per-GB data transfer premium on top of normal data transfer out. Cost goes up.
o.C: Savings Plans discount compute, not data transfer. Bigger instances add cost.
o.D: Every Region still pays internet data transfer out, and running three more copies multiplies compute cost.
